query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A new multi‐scale predictive model that explicitly incorporates atomic-scale mass and force‐constant disorder will predict that, in defect‐free (or oxygen‐minimized) HfNbTaTiZr, the lattice thermal conductivity deviates from standard Debye‐model predictions. Specifically, at high temperatures (300–1200 K) the lattice conductivity is reduced by roughly a modest fraction due to enhanced anharmonic phonon scattering from force‐constant fluctuations, while at low temperatures (<200 K) the lattice and electronic contributions become comparable. This approach operates by capturing the mediator effect of random force-constant fluctuations that enhance anharmonic phonon scattering.
generation.material_initial_state: A single‐phase, defect‐free (or minimally oxygen-contaminated, e.g., <0.1 wt% O) HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy.
generation.intervention: Application of a new predictive approach that combines atomistic (e.g., MD and/or DFT) simulations with machine learning to separately quantify the lattice (phonon) and electronic heat transport contributions by explicitly modeling force-constant (anharmonic) and mass disorder effects.
generation.conditions: Measurements and predictions performed on bulk, chemically homogeneous HfNbTaTiZr with tightly controlled impurity levels; studies conducted at low temperatures below a designated threshold and at high temperatures over a broad range as specified in the question.
generation.structural_mediator: Random atomic-scale fluctuations in force constants and masses due to the inherent disorder in the high-entropy alloy lattice.
generation.mechanism: The random distribution of different elements introduces significant anharmonicity via force‐constant fluctuations and severe lattice distortion from multicomponent mixing, which strongly scatter phonons. This yields a lattice thermal conductivity that does not follow standard T^(-1) scaling and is notably lower than predictions for perfect, defect‐free crystals, while also leading to a balance between lattice and electronic contributions at low temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: At 300–1200 K the lattice thermal conductivity (κ_lattice) will be approximately 20–30% lower than that predicted by conventional analytical techniques based on Debye temperature estimates of perfect crystals. Below 200 K, the lattice-derived and electronic contributions to total thermal conductivity will be of similar magnitude, contrasting with the electron-dominated transport usually assumed for metals.
generation.baseline: Existing analytical and DFT-derived conductivity estimates for perfect, defect-free bulk crystals that rely on standard Debye and mass-disorder models, which tend to overestimate lattice κ by neglecting complex force-constant fluctuations.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to well-synthesized, bulk HfNbTaTiZr with minimal oxygen or defect-induced scattering. In samples with significant grain boundaries, high impurity levels, or additional defects, the interplay of scattering mechanisms may deviate from the model predictions.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative improvement (20–30% reduction) is an approximate range based on expected force-constant fluctuation effects; actual values may vary with sample purity and measurement technique. Moreover, accurately isolating lattice from electronic conductivity in experiments can introduce uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare high-purity HfNbTaTiZr samples with oxygen content controlled below 0.1 wt%. Employ thermal diffusivity measurements (e.g., via laser flash) combined with precise electrical resistivity measurements to separately evaluate the lattice and electronic contributions to total thermal conductivity. Use low-temperature heat capacity and resistivity techniques to determine contributions below 200 K, and high-temperature measurements (300–1200 K) to compare total conductivity with predictions.
measurements: Electrical conductivity (for estimating κ_e via the Wiedemann-Franz law)
Atomic-scale structural characterization (to confirm defect-free status)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental lattice thermal conductivity at 300–1200 K does not show an approximate 20–30% reduction relative to conventional Debye-based predictions, or if below 200 K the lattice and electronic contributions are not observed to be comparable, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Based on the existing simulation results, this paper reduces the atomic content of Ta and Hf at the same time to investigate their effects on the mechanical properties of the HEA, the tensile stress–strain curve obtained from the simulation is shown in Figure 4d. On the other hand, to further verify the accuracy of the simulation results, as-cast HfxNbTaxTiZr HEA samples (x = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) were prepared and tested to compare with the simulation results. The tensile stress–strain curve obtained from the test is shown in Figure 4e. The tensile yield strengths of HEAs with different compositions were calculated based on the simulation curves and compared with the tensile strengths obtained by testing. The comparison results are shown in Figure 4f. It can be seen from the comparison results that the variation trend of the simulated values is in line with the actual test results. The variation trend of dislocation density shown in Figure 5 also provides evidence.

Thermal conductivity (κ) is usually divided into two components, the electronic thermal conductivity (κe) and the lattice thermal conductivity (κg). Direct experimental separation of these two components is not feasible. Thus, to the first order approximation, κe is usually estimated based on the Wiedemann-Franz relationship where L is the Lorentz constant of 2.45 × 10−8 W Ω K−2 .

Recently, a new family of crystalline metallic materials has been discovered and has come to the forefront of materials research for their exceptional mechanical properties: High-Entropy Alloys (HEAs). Obtained with casting techniques from the melt, HEAs are single-phase, equiatomic alloys with four or more elements that are evenly dispersed in an average ordered, close-packed, and simple crystalline structure, forming a random solid solution,. The strong chemical disorder within the unit cell introduces disorder at a larger lengthscale, as the periodically repeated unit cell is in fact always different due to the random atomic arrangement within it. As such, the translational invariance is disrupted, drawing these materials closer to glasses. Indeed, HEAs share with these latter the presence of a distribution in atomic sizes, masses and force-constants, usually absent or present only in a limited extent in crystalline materials. Moreover, HEAs also exhibit thermal transport properties quite similar to glasses: thermal conductivities that are much lower than in simple metals, going from some tens of W/mK down to less than 2 W/mK, and a low and almost temperature independent lattice
